events.c: The crew reported ready for takeoff, waiting before the runway.
The tower cleared the aircraft to take off from runway 22R.
The aircraft’s ground sensor switched to airborne, marking takeoff.
Controllers cleared the aircraft to climb and handed it over to New York Center.
Controllers cleared the aircraft toward the DOVEY navigation point and allowed a further climb.
The relief first officer took the right seat. The exact time isn’t known.
The controller cleared an Atlantic crossing route, and the crew repeated the instructions back.
The aircraft leveled off at its assigned cruise level.
The captain checked in on a new radio frequency. This was the aircraft’s last received transmission.
The captain announced a brief bathroom visit. Seat and door sounds followed.
A sound resembling the cockpit door operating was recorded.
A brief comment was recorded, but its words and language remain unknown.
The relief first officer spoke quietly. No aircraft problem had been identified before this statement.
A sound resembling an electric seat motor was recorded. Its purpose is unknown.
The autopilot disengaged. No disconnect warning tone was heard.
The relief first officer repeated a quiet phrase. The words alone do not establish a motive or emergency.
The engine power levers moved to idle.
Both tail controls moved downward, and the aircraft began lowering its nose.
Four caution tones sounded. Their specific cause is unknown.
Both tail controls moved farther downward at about this time.
The captain’s voice was recorded as he returned to the cockpit.
A warning began as the aircraft exceeded its speed limit. It continued until the recording ended.
The aircraft’s nose pointed about 40 degrees below level, its lowest recorded angle.
Both tail controls began moving to raise the nose. The descent then slowed.
The aircraft’s fastest descent was estimated at about 39,000 feet per minute.
The right engine’s fuel lever moved to cutoff. Who moved it is unknown.
At about this time, the left tail control raised the nose while the right pushed it down.
The left engine’s fuel lever moved to cutoff. Both engines slowed, later cutting electrical power to the recorders.
The aircraft’s peak speed was estimated at nearly the speed of sound.
The engine power levers moved forward, but the separate fuel controls remained shut off.
The captain asked whether the engines had been shut down.
The handle for the wing’s braking panels reached nearly full deployment. The panels’ actual positions are unknown.
The left tail control pointed upward while the right pointed downward. Pilot control movements were not recorded.
The captain repeatedly asked the other pilot to help pull back on the controls.
Nantucket received the aircraft’s last radar signal sent by its onboard transmitter.
The flight recorder stopped recording flight data.
The first dive ended near an estimated 16,000 feet, followed by a climb.
The cockpit voice recording ended before the aircraft struck the ocean.
The aircraft climbed to about 25,000 feet and turned before descending again.
New York Center received its last radar echo. Earlier target markers remained on the display.
The aircraft struck the ocean at about this time. The exact impact time is unknown.
The controller reported lost radar contact and requested a reset of the aircraft’s radar transmitter. No response came.
The area manager notified Air Force and Coast Guard rescue authorities.
The Navy recovered the flight recorder on November 9, 1999, and sent it to investigators.
Egyptian investigators left the cause unresolved, considered a tail control defect likely, and rejected an intentional crash.
U.S. investigators attributed the crash to the relief first officer’s control movements. His reason remains unknown.

one_line: A Boeing 767 dived, briefly climbed, then struck the Atlantic, killing all 217 aboard.
status_why: U.S. investigators blamed the relief first officer’s control movements; Egyptian investigators disputed that conclusion and sought further mechanical investigation.
